content:
You are a knowledge compiler. Your job is to read a daily conversation log
and extract knowledge into structured wiki articles.

## Schema (AGENTS.md)

# AGENTS.md - Personal Knowledge Base Schema

> Adapted from [Andrej Karpathy's LLM Knowledge Base](https://gist.github.com/karpathy/442a6bf555914893e9891c11519de94f) architecture.
> Instead of ingesting external articles, this system compiles knowledge from your own AI conversations.

## The Compiler Analogy

```
daily/          = source code    (your conversations - the raw material)
LLM             = compiler       (extracts and organizes knowledge)
knowledge/      = executable     (structured, queryable knowledge base)
lint            = test suite     (health checks for consistency)
memlint         = test suite     (same, for the memory files loaded each session)
queries         = runtime        (using the knowledge)
```

You don't manually organize your knowledge. You have conversations, and the LLM handles the synthesis, cross-referencing, and maintenance.

---

## Architecture

### Layer 1: `daily/` - Conversation Logs (Immutable Source)

Daily logs capture what happened in your AI coding sessions. These are the "raw sources" - append-only, never edited after the fact.

```
daily/
├── 2026-04-01.md
├── 2026-04-02.md
├── ...
```

Each file follows this format:

```markdown
# Daily Log: YYYY-MM-DD

## Sessions

### Session (HH:MM) - Brief Title

**Context:** What the user was working on.

**Key Exchanges:**
- User asked about X, assistant explained Y
- Decided to use Z approach because...
- Discovered that W doesn't work when...

**Decisions Made:**
- Chose library X over Y because...
- Architecture: went with pattern Z

**Lessons Learned:**
- Always do X before Y to avoid...
- The gotcha with Z is that...

**Action Items:**
- [ ] Follow up on X
- [ ] Refactor Y when time permits
```

### Layer 2: `knowledge/` - Compiled Knowledge (LLM-Owned)

The LLM owns this directory entirely. Humans read it but rarely edit it directly.

```
knowledge/
├── index.md              # Master catalog - every article with one-line summary
├── log.md                # Append-only chronological build log
├── concepts/             # Atomic knowledge articles
├── connections/          # Cross-cutting insights linking 2+ concepts
└── qa/                   # Filed query answers (compounding knowledge)
```

### Layer 3: This File (AGENTS.md)

The schema that tells the LLM how to compile and maintain the knowledge base. This is the "compiler specification."

---

## Structural Files

### `knowledge/index.md` - Master Catalog

A table listing every knowledge article. This is the primary retrieval mechanism - the LLM reads this FIRST when answering any query, then selects relevant articles to read in full.

Format:

```markdown
# Knowledge Base Index

| Article | Summary | Compiled From | Updated |
|---------|---------|---------------|---------|
| [[concepts/supabase-auth]] | Row-level security patterns and JWT gotchas | daily/2026-04-02.md | 2026-04-02 |
| [[connections/auth-and-webhooks]] | Token verification patterns shared across Supabase auth and Stripe webhooks | daily/2026-04-02.md, daily/2026-04-04.md | 2026-04-04 |
```

### `knowledge/log.md` - Build Log

Append-only chronological record of every compile, query, and lint operation.

Format:

```markdown
# Build Log

## [2026-04-01T14:30:00] compile | Daily Log 2026-04-01
- Source: daily/2026-04-01.md
- Articles created: [[concepts/nextjs-project-structure]], [[concepts/tailwind-setup]]
- Articles updated: (none)

## [2026-04-02T09:00:00] query | "How do I handle auth redirects?"
- Consulted: [[concepts/supabase-auth]], [[concepts/nextjs-middleware]]
- Filed to: [[qa/auth-redirect-handling]]
```

---

## Article Formats

### Concept Articles (`knowledge/concepts/`)

One article per atomic piece of knowledge. These are facts, patterns, decisions, preferences, and lessons extracted from your conversations.

```markdown
---
title: "Concept Name"
aliases: [alternate-name, abbreviation]
tags: [domain, topic]
sources:
  - "daily/2026-04-01.md"
  - "daily/2026-04-03.md"
created: 2026-04-01
updated: 2026-04-03
---

# Concept Name

[2-4 sentence core explanation]

## Key Points

- [Bullet points, each self-contained]

## Details

[Deeper explanation, encyclopedia-style paragraphs]

## Related Concepts

- [[concepts/related-concept]] - How it connects

## Sources

- [[daily/2026-04-01.md]] - Initial discovery during project setup
- [[daily/2026-04-03.md]] - Updated after debugging session
```

### Connection Articles (`knowledge/connections/`)

Cross-cutting synthesis linking 2+ concepts. Created when a conversation reveals a non-obvious relationship.

```markdown
---
title: "Connection: X and Y"
connects:
  - "concepts/concept-x"
  - "concepts/concept-y"
sources:
  - "daily/2026-04-04.md"
created: 2026-04-04
updated: 2026-04-04
---

# Connection: X and Y

## The Connection

[What links these concepts]

## Key Insight

[The non-obvious relationship discovered]

## Evidence

[Specific examples from conversations]

## Related Concepts

- [[concepts/concept-x]]
- [[concepts/concept-y]]
```

### Q&A Articles (`knowledge/qa/`)

Filed answers from queries. Every complex question answered by the system can be permanently stored, making future queries smarter.

```markdown
---
title: "Q: Original Question"
question: "The exact question asked"
consulted:
  - "concepts/article-1"
  - "concepts/article-2"
filed: 2026-04-05
---

# Q: Original Question

## Answer

[The synthesized answer with [[wikilinks]] to sources]

## Sources Consulted

- [[concepts/article-1]] - Relevant because...
- [[concepts/article-2]] - Provided context on...

## Follow-Up Questions

- What about edge case X?
- How does this change if Y?
```

---

## Core Operations

### 1. Compile (daily/ -> knowledge/)

When processing a daily log:

1. Read the daily log file
2. Read `knowledge/index.md` to understand current knowledge state
3. Read existing articles that may need updating
4. For each piece of knowledge found in the log:
   - If an existing concept article covers this topic: UPDATE it with new information, add the daily log as a source
   - If it's a new topic: CREATE a new `concepts/` article
5. If the log reveals a non-obvious connection between 2+ existing concepts: CREATE a `connections/` article
6. UPDATE `knowledge/index.md` with new/modified entries
7. APPEND to `knowledge/log.md`

**Important guidelines:**
- A single daily log may touch 3-10 knowledge articles
- Prefer updating existing articles over creating near-duplicates
- Use Obsidian-style `[[wikilinks]]` with full relative paths from knowledge/
- Write in encyclopedia style - factual, concise, self-contained
- Every article must have YAML frontmatter
- Every article must link back to its source daily logs

### 2. Query (Ask the Knowledge Base)

1. Read `knowledge/index.md` (the master catalog)
2. Based on the question, identify 3-10 relevant articles from the index
3. Read those articles in full
4. Synthesize an answer with `[[wikilink]]` citations
5. If `--file-back` is specified: create a `knowledge/qa/` article and update index.md and log.md

**Why this works without RAG:** At personal knowledge base scale (50-500 articles), the LLM reading a structured index outperforms cosine similarity. The LLM understands what the question is really asking and selects pages accordingly. Embeddings find similar words; the LLM finds relevant concepts.

### 3. Lint (Health Checks)

Seven checks, run periodically:

1. **Broken links** - `[[wikilinks]]` pointing to non-existent articles
2. **Orphan pages** - Articles with zero inbound links from other articles
3. **Orphan sources** - Daily logs that haven't been compiled yet
4. **Stale articles** - Source daily log changed since article was last compiled
5. **Contradictions** - Conflicting claims across articles (requires LLM judgment)
6. **Missing backlinks** - A links to B but B doesn't link back to A
7. **Sparse articles** - Below 200 words, likely incomplete

Output: a markdown report with severity levels (error, warning, suggestion).

---

## Conventions

- **Wikilinks:** Use Obsidian-style `[[path/to/article]]` without `.md` extension
- **Writing style:** Encyclopedia-style, factual, third-person where appropriate
- **Dates:** ISO 8601 (YYYY-MM-DD for dates, full ISO for timestamps in log.md)
- **File naming:** lowercase, hyphens for spaces (e.g., `supabase-row-level-security.md`)
- **Frontmatter:** Every article must have YAML frontmatter with at minimum: title, sources, created, updated
- **Sources:** Always link back to the daily log(s) that contributed to an article

---

## Full Project Structure

```
llm-personal-kb/
|-- .claude/
|   |-- settings.json                # Hook configuration (auto-activates in Claude Code)
|-- .gitignore                       # Excludes runtime state, temp files, caches
|-- AGENTS.md                        # This file - schema + full technical reference
|-- README.md                        # Concise overview + quick start
|-- pyproject.toml                   # Dependencies (at root so hooks can find it)
|-- daily/                           # "Source code" - conversation logs (immutable)
|-- knowledge/                       # "Executable" - compiled knowledge (LLM-owned)
|   |-- index.md                     #   Master catalog - THE retrieval mechanism
|   |-- log.md                       #   Append-only build log
|   |-- concepts/                    #   Atomic knowledge articles
|   |-- connections/                 #   Cross-cutting insights linking 2+ concepts
|   |-- qa/                          #   Filed query answers (compounding knowledge)
|-- scripts/                         # CLI tools
|   |-- compile.py                   #   Compile daily logs -> knowledge articles
|   |-- query.py                     #   Ask questions (index-guided, no RAG)
|   |-- lint.py                      #   7 health checks (knowledge base)
|   |-- memlint.py                   #   6 health checks (memory tier)
|   |-- flush.py                     #   Extract memories from conversations (background)
|   |-- config.py                    #   Path constants
|   |-- utils.py                     #   Shared helpers
|-- hooks/                           # Claude Code hooks
|   |-- session-start.py             #   Injects knowledge into every session
|   |-- session-end.py               #   Extracts conversation -> daily log
|   |-- pre-compact.py               #   Safety net: captures context before compaction
|-- reports/                         # Lint reports (gitignored)
```

---

## Hook System (Automatic Capture)

Hooks are configured in `.claude/settings.json` and fire automatically when you use Claude Code in this project.

### `.claude/settings.json` Format

```json
{
  "hooks": {
    "SessionStart": [{ "matcher": "", "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "command": "uv run python hooks/session-start.py", "timeout": 15 }] }],
    "PreCompact": [{ "matcher": "", "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "command": "uv run python hooks/pre-compact.py", "timeout": 10 }] }],
    "SessionEnd": [{ "matcher": "", "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "command": "uv run python hooks/session-end.py", "timeout": 10 }] }]
  }
}
```

Commands use simple relative paths from the project root. Empty `matcher` catches all events.

### Hook Details

**`session-start.py`** (SessionStart)
- Pure local I/O, no API calls, runs in under 1 second
- Reads `knowledge/index.md` and the most recent daily log
- Outputs JSON to stdout: `{"hookSpecificOutput": {"hookEventName": "SessionStart", "additionalContext": "..."}}`
- Claude sees the knowledge base index at the start of every session
- Max context: 20,000 characters

**`session-end.py`** (SessionEnd)
- Reads hook input from stdin (JSON with `session_id`, `transcript_path`, `cwd`)
- Copies the raw JSONL transcript to a temp file (no parsing in the hook - keeps it fast)
- Spawns `flush.py` as a fully detached background process
- Recursion guard: exits immediately if `CLAUDE_INVOKED_BY` env var is set

**`pre-compact.py`** (PreCompact)
- Same architecture as session-end.py
- Fires before Claude Code auto-compacts the context window
- Guards against empty `transcript_path` (known Claude Code bug #13668)
- Critical for long sessions: captures context before summarization discards it

**Why both PreCompact and SessionEnd?** Long-running sessions may trigger multiple auto-compactions before you close the session. Without PreCompact, intermediate context is lost to summarization before SessionEnd ever fires.

### Background Flush Process (`flush.py`)

Spawned by both hooks as a fully detached background process:
- **Windows:** `CREATE_NEW_PROCESS_GROUP | DETACHED_PROCESS` flags
- **Mac/Linux:** `start_new_session=True`

This ensures flush.py survives after Claude Code's hook process exits.

**What flush.py does:**
1. Sets `CLAUDE_INVOKED_BY=memory_flush` env var (prevents recursive hook firing)
2. Reads the pre-extracted conversation context from the temp `.md` file
3. Skips if context is empty or if same session was flushed within 60 seconds (deduplication)
4. Calls Claude Agent SDK (`query()` with `allowed_tools=[]`, `max_turns=2`)
5. Claude decides what's worth saving - returns structured bullet points or `FLUSH_OK`
6. Appends result to `daily/YYYY-MM-DD.md`
7. Cleans up temp context file
8. **End-of-day auto-compilation:** If it's past 6 PM local time (`COMPILE_AFTER_HOUR = 18`) and today's daily log has changed since its last compilation (hash comparison against `state.json`), spawns `compile.py` as another detached background process. This means compilation happens automatically once a day without needing a cron job or manual trigger.

### JSONL Transcript Format

Claude Code stores conversations as `.jsonl` files. Messages are nested under a `message` key:

```python
entry = json.loads(line)
msg = entry.get("message", {})
role = msg.get("role", "")     # "user" or "assistant"
content = msg.get("content", "")  # string or list of content blocks
```

Content can be a string or a list of blocks (`{"type": "text", "text": "..."}` dicts).

---

## Script Details

### compile.py - The Compiler

Uses the Claude Agent SDK's async streaming `query()`:

```python
async for message in query(
    prompt=compile_prompt,
    options=ClaudeAgentOptions(
        cwd=str(ROOT_DIR),
        system_prompt={"type": "preset", "preset": "claude_code"},
        allowed_tools=["Read", "Write", "Edit", "Glob", "Grep"],
        permission_mode="acceptEdits",
        max_turns=30,
    ),
):
```

- Builds a prompt with: AGENTS.md schema, current index, all existing articles, and the daily log
- Claude reads the daily log, decides what concepts to extract, and writes files directly
- `permission_mode="acceptEdits"` auto-approves all file operations
- Incremental: tracks SHA-256 hashes of daily logs in `state.json`, skips unchanged files
- Cost: ~$0.45-0.65 per daily log (increases as KB grows)

**CLI:**
```bash
uv run python scripts/compile.py              # compile new/changed only
uv run python scripts/compile.py --all        # force recompile everything
uv run python scripts/compile.py --file daily/2026-04-01.md
uv run python scripts/compile.py --dry-run
```

### query.py - Index-Guided Retrieval

Loads the entire knowledge base into context (index + all articles). No RAG.

At personal KB scale (50-500 articles), the LLM reading a structured index outperforms vector similarity. The LLM understands what you're really asking; cosine similarity just finds similar words.

**CLI:**
```bash
uv run python scripts/query.py "What auth patterns do I use?"
uv run python scripts/query.py "What's my error handling strategy?" --file-back
```

With `--file-back`, creates a Q&A article in `knowledge/qa/` and updates the index and log. This is the compounding loop - every question makes the KB smarter.

### lint.py - Health Checks

Seven checks:

| Check | Type | Catches |
|-------|------|---------|
| Broken links | Structural | `[[wikilinks]]` to non-existent articles |
| Orphan pages | Structural | Articles with zero inbound links |
| Orphan sources | Structural | Daily logs not yet compiled |
| Stale articles | Structural | Source logs changed since compilation |
| Missing backlinks | Structural | A links to B but B doesn't link back |
| Sparse articles | Structural | Under 200 words |
| Contradictions | LLM | Conflicting claims across articles |

**CLI:**
```bash
uv run python scripts/lint.py                    # all checks
uv run python scripts/lint.py --structural-only  # skip LLM check (free)
```

Reports saved to `reports/lint-YYYY-MM-DD.md`.

### memlint.py - Memory Tier Health Checks

`lint.py` stops at `knowledge/`. The files the harness actually injects into every
session live elsewhere and were never audited: `~/.claude/global-memory/` and the
active `~/.claude/projects/*/memory/` slugs. Drift there is the most expensive
drift in the system, because it is read at the start of every conversation.

Seven checks:

| Check | Type | Catches |
|-------|------|---------|
| Index drift | Structural | Memory file missing from MEMORY.md, or an index pointer with no file |
| Broken links | Structural | `[[links]]` that do not match any frontmatter `name:` in the slug |
| Name form | Structural | `name:` that is not the bare kebab stem (type belongs in `metadata.type`) |
| Near-duplicates | Structural | Within-slug TF-IDF similarity above the threshold |
| Cap overruns | Structural | A file past the character cap it declares in its own header |
| Content in index | Structural | Facts written into MEMORY.md, which is meant to hold pointers |
| Contradictions | LLM | Conflicting, redundant, or superseded claims across memory files |

**Scope.** Retired `C--Users-eric-rash*` slugs are excluded everywhere - the macOS
slugs were re-keyed from them, so including them reports history as duplication.
`handoffs/` and `transcripts/` are session records, not memory, and are never linted.
The LLM check defaults to `global-memory` + the `DEV` and `~` slugs, the ones that
load together in a working session; `--all-slugs` widens it.

**Similarity threshold.** Default 0.45. Measured 2026-09-01: the highest genuine
within-slug pair scored 0.33. The report always prints the top pairs per slug so
the number can be retuned against evidence.

**Report only.** memlint never edits a memory file. Merging and deleting memories
stays a human decision.

**CLI:**
```bash
uv run python scripts/memlint.py                    # all checks
uv run python scripts/memlint.py --structural-only  # skip LLM check (free)
uv run python scripts/memlint.py --all-slugs        # widen the LLM check
uv run python scripts/memlint.py --threshold 0.6    # retune near-duplicates
```

Reports saved to `reports/memlint-YYYY-MM-DD.md`; `--structural-only` writes
`memlint-YYYY-MM-DD-structural.md` instead, so a free run never clobbers the
day's paid-for LLM findings. Runs automatically after the Sunday 02:30
adjudication job.

---

## State Tracking

`scripts/state.json` tracks:
- `ingested` - map of daily log filenames to SHA-256 hashes, compilation timestamps, and costs
- `query_count` - total queries run
- `last_lint` - timestamp of most recent lint
- `last_memlint` - timestamp of most recent memory-tier lint
- `total_cost` - cumulative API cost

`scripts/last-flush.json` tracks flush deduplication (session_id + timestamp).

Both are gitignored and regenerated automatically.

---

## Dependencies

`pyproject.toml` (at project root):
- `claude-agent-sdk>=0.1.29` - Claude Agent SDK for LLM calls with tool use
- `python-dotenv>=1.0.0` - Environment variable management
- `tzdata>=2024.1` - Timezone data
- Python 3.12+, managed by [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/)

No API key needed - uses Claude Code's built-in credentials at `~/.claude/.credentials.json`.

---

## Costs

| Operation | Cost |
|-----------|------|
| Compile one daily log | $0.45-0.65 |
| Query (no file-back) | ~$0.15-0.25 |
| Query (with file-back) | ~$0.25-0.40 |
| Full lint (with contradictions) | ~$0.15-0.25 |
| Structural lint only | $0.00 |
| Full memlint (with contradictions) | ~$0.15-0.25 |
| Structural memlint only | $0.00 |
| Memory flush (per session) | ~$0.02-0.05 |

---

## Customization

### Additional Article Types

Add directories like `people/`, `projects/`, `tools/` to `knowledge/`. Define the article format in this file (AGENTS.md) and update `utils.py`'s `list_wiki_articles()` to include them.

### Obsidian Integration

The knowledge base is pure markdown with `[[wikilinks]]` - works natively in Obsidian. Point a vault at `knowledge/` for graph view, backlinks, and search.

### Scaling Beyond Index-Guided Retrieval

At ~2,000+ articles / ~2M+ tokens, the index becomes too large for the context window. At that point, add hybrid RAG (keyword + semantic search) as a retrieval layer before the LLM. See Karpathy's recommendation of `qmd` by Tobi Lutke for search at scale.

# Scratch-Folder Artifacts Die With the Job

During the 2026-09-01 `~/DEV` graph refresh, fifteen operational scripts and two Codex verification reports were found living inside a disposable job scratch folder — a location that is removed when the job ends, taking the artifacts with it. All were relocated to durable paths under `~/DEV/graphify-out/` (scripts to `scripts/`, reports alongside the graph output), and the shell wrappers that invoked them were repointed because they still held stale scratch paths. The daily log notes this was "a trap already flagged in user's notes," making it a repeat occurrence rather than a first discovery — and the 2026-08-30 coach-report prototype session had hit the same trap two days earlier.

## Key Points

- **Scratch folders are defined by the system as not surviving the job.** Anything whose value outlives the run — scripts, verification reports, resume instructions — must be written elsewhere at creation time, not rescued afterward.
- **Relocation is incomplete without repointing the callers.** The shell wrappers still referenced the old scratch paths after the scripts moved; a move that leaves stale references produces a broken toolchain rather than a durable one.
- **Handoff documents must reference durable paths.** The Codex reports were copied out of scratch specifically so the handoff would point at locations that still exist when the handoff is read.
- **This is a recurring trap across unrelated projects.** On 2026-08-30 the coach-report prototypes' build scripts — notably `build_payloads.py`, which keeps opponent names and dates out of the markup — were found in the job's scratch folder and flagged for relocation into `~/DEV/Football/CoachReport_Prototypes/`. Its recurrence indicates the failure is structural, so the remedy is a default write location, not vigilance.
- **The same sessions that corrected the trap reproduced it in their own handoffs:** `/var/folders/gw/.../T/handoff-baylor-coach-report-2026-08-30.md` on 8-30 and `handoff-arms-graph-2026-08-31.md` on 9-01, both temp paths.

## Details

The mechanism is identical to the `/tmp` handoff loss documented in [[concepts/handoff-document-placement-discipline]], generalized from one document type to a whole class of artifacts. A scratch or temp directory is attractive at write time because it is unconditionally writable and requires no decision about where a file belongs; the cost is deferred entirely to the future moment when someone needs the file and it is gone. Scripts are a particularly bad fit for scratch because they are, by definition, the things you will want to run *again* — a fifteen-script toolchain in a disposable folder is a toolchain with a scheduled expiry, and a payload builder like `build_payloads.py` encodes a data-hygiene decision (keeping opponent names and dates out of the markup) that would have to be rediscovered if lost. The correct default is to write anything invocable or referenceable into the project tree next to the work it operates on, which is exactly where both relocations landed: `~/DEV/graphify-out/scripts/` and `~/DEV/Football/CoachReport_Prototypes/`.

The wrapper-repointing detail is the part most easily missed. Moving files to durable storage changes where they live but not what refers to them, and the shell wrappers had hardcoded scratch paths that survived the move as dangling references. A half-completed relocation is arguably worse than no relocation, because the artifacts now appear safe while the entry points into them are broken — the failure surfaces later, at invocation time, rather than at move time. The general rule is that durability work must sweep the reference graph, not just the files: after moving an artifact, grep for the old path and update every caller before considering the move done.

That two sessions two days apart both corrected this trap and reproduced it — relocating scripts out of scratch while writing their own handoffs into `/var/folders/.../T/` — is the strongest evidence that the fix cannot be attention. Each location was chosen by different reasoning at a different moment, and the temp path won every time nothing forced the question. A durable default (a project-local `handoffs/` or the project tree itself) removes the decision entirely, in the same way that deriving a backup manifest from a directory scan removes the omission failure mode in [[concepts/backup-manifest-drift-and-launchd-status-lag]].

# Claude Code System Health Check and Remediation Session

On 2026-06-25, a system health-check and remediation session worked through four flagged maintenance items — memsearch/Milvus timeout tuning, memory-compiler SDK upgrade, calendar auth, and a memory-injection audit — plus a cleanup of the resolved-error noise in `.errors.log`. The session raised memsearch's timeout thresholds, upgraded `claude-agent-sdk`, trimmed the Tier A auto-injection index from 15 to 10 files for token savings, and cleared an overdue pending decision from global memory.

## Key Points

- **memsearch timeout raised, two layers in sync:** the internal timeout in `memsearch-sync.js` was raised 25s→45s, and the `settings.json` hook's outer limit was raised 28s→50s to match. The outer hook limit must exceed the internal timeout or the hook is killed before memsearch can complete.
- **claude-agent-sdk upgraded 0.2.101→0.2.110** in `~/.claude/claude-memory-compiler` to fix flush-failed errors — a continuation of the version-skew maintenance pattern (see [[concepts/claude-memory-compiler-setup]]).
- **Tier A auto-injection index trimmed 15→10 files:** four files (Zotero CLI, AI Integration Initiative, Athlete Data Governance, Sport Science Symposium) were removed from auto-injection but kept on disk (still memsearch-searchable). Estimated token savings ~8,800→~6,700 injected per session.
- **Milvus was healthy the whole time:** the ETIMEDOUT errors were a memsearch spawn/timeout issue, not a Milvus outage — the obvious culprit (the vector DB) was not the cause. Milvus ran healthy in Docker throughout.
- **Overdue pending decision cleared:** the stale "memory injection cost audit" pending decision was removed from global MEMORY.md and replaced with an OKR Q1 gate review dated 8/31; `.errors.log` was cleared of resolved ETIMEDOUT noise from 6/12–6/24.

## Details

The session illustrates a recurring maintenance discipline: periodically working through flagged health-check items in a single dedicated pass rather than letting them accumulate. The memsearch timeout tuning addressed the ETIMEDOUT noise that had been accumulating in `.errors.log` since mid-June (see [[concepts/memsearch-tool-maintenance]] for the concurrent-contention ETIMEDOUT pattern). Critically, the fix required adjusting two coordinated limits — the internal memsearch timeout and the outer hook timeout in `settings.json` — keeping the outer limit strictly larger so the hook does not terminate memsearch mid-operation. The diagnostic lesson was to not assume the obvious culprit: Milvus, the vector database memsearch depends on, was healthy in Docker the entire time; the timeouts originated in memsearch's own spawn/timeout behavior.

The Tier A index trimming is a token-efficiency operation on the memory-injection layer. The global MEMORY.md indexes Tier A project files for auto-injection at session start; as that index grows, each session pays a larger fixed token cost. Trimming the index from 15 to 10 files (removing four lower-priority project files from auto-injection while leaving them on disk) reduced the estimated per-session injection cost from ~8,800 to ~6,700 tokens. Because the removed files remain on disk and memsearch-searchable, no information is lost — only the always-on injection footprint is reduced, following the same Tier A/Tier B capacity-management logic documented in [[concepts/claude-code-memory-architecture]]. A notable operational constraint surfaced during the session: the auto-mode classifier blocks edits to files under `.claude/` (including `settings.json` and per-project MEMORY.md files) even when those files are personal notes rather than active configuration. Such edits require an explicit user "go ahead," and some operations (like `Clear-Content` on `.errors.log`) must be run manually by the user because the classifier will not permit the agent to perform them.

# `synced (ahead=0)` Does Not Mean Today's Edits Are Committed

A 2026-09-07 config-hygiene session left every edit uncommitted on the expectation that the 09:00 nightly backup would commit and push the skills repo automatically. The session recorded two adjacent status-reading traps: `synced (ahead=0)` reports that nothing is *queued to push*, which is trivially true when nothing has been committed at all; and `com.keystone.dailybackup`'s exit code 1 is stale and clears only on a launchd-initiated run, so manual `/backup` invocations leave it red regardless of outcome.

## Key Points

- **`ahead=0` counts committed-but-unpushed commits.** A working tree full of uncommitted edits produces the same `synced (ahead=0)` as a genuinely clean, fully-backed-up repository — the indicator is blind to the working tree.
- **Deferring commits to the nightly job is a deliberate, defensible choice** (it avoids duplicating the automation's work), but it means the window between the edit and 09:00 has the edits on exactly one disk while the sync indicator reads green. Both of this evening's sessions — the config edits and the `MEMORY.md` trim — were left in that window simultaneously.
- **A stale launchd exit code only clears on a launchd-initiated run.** Manual `/backup` invocations do not reset `com.keystone.dailybackup`'s column-2 status, which stays 1 until the next scheduled tick or an explicit `launchctl kickstart`.
- **The forcing option was named explicitly:** `launchctl kickstart -k gui/$(id -u)/com.keystone.dailybackup` (~7 minutes) versus simply waiting for 09:00. The question was left open with the user rather than decided unilaterally.
- **Unexplained extra runs are worth chasing to a cause.** Additional 07:00 and 07:11 backup runs were resolved as manual user invocations rather than a scheduling defect — a benign explanation, but only after checking.
- **A rollback path was recorded alongside the change:** `git -C ~/.claude checkout CLAUDE.md AGENTS.md .gitignore && rm ~/.claude/TOOLPATHS.md`, with the prior DEV file backed up under the session's job tmp directory.

## Details

The `ahead=0` misreading belongs to the family of status fields whose predicate is narrower than the question being asked of them, described in [[connections/status-field-scope-narrower-than-the-question]]. The field faithfully answers "are there local commits the remote lacks?" and is read as "is my work backed up?" The two coincide only when the working tree is clean, and the deferred-commit workflow adopted here guarantees they diverge for most of the day. The practical consequence is that a durability check must inspect the working tree — `git status`, not the ahead/behind counter — and that the answer to "is today's work safe?" during the deferral window is genuinely no, at least until the CRASHBOX SSD leg captures uncommitted files as documented in [[concepts/on-demand-backup-skill-and-ssd-completeness]]. That leg exists precisely for this class of content, which is why its completeness matters more on days like this one, when a full evening of `~/.claude` and `~/DEV` edits sat uncommitted by design.

The launchd exit-code behavior restates and sharpens the finding from [[concepts/backup-manifest-drift-and-launchd-status-lag]]: column 2 tracks scheduled invocations only. The new detail is the escape hatch — `launchctl kickstart -k` initiates a run *through launchd*, so unlike a manual `/backup` it does update the status field, at the cost of about seven minutes. That gives a genuine choice rather than a resignation: wait for the schedule and let the code self-clear, or force a launchd-initiated run that both commits the day's edits and resets the indicator in one pass. The session correctly framed this as a decision for the user, since the tradeoff is between latency and a few minutes of machine time, not between correct and incorrect.

The extra-runs investigation is a small but instructive counterpoint to the session's other findings. Two unexplained backup executions at 07:00 and 07:11 could plausibly have been a duplicate trigger, a retry loop, or a misconfigured plist — all defects worth fixing. The actual cause was the user running them by hand. The cheapest resolution to an anomaly in a scheduled system is often to ask whether a human caused it, and doing so before instrumenting the scheduler avoids the failure mode where a benign event drives a real change to working automation. Recording the rollback command in the same breath as the change is the complementary habit: it is cheapest to write down while the change set is still in working memory, and it is the only thing that makes an uncommitted, unbacked-up edit set safely reversible.

# Distinguishing Stale from Live Entries Before Clearing an Error Log

The `~/.claude/global-memory/transcripts/.errors.log` file is the asynchronous escalation channel through which scheduled jobs surface failures to the next interactive session. Because it is append-only and read at session start, it accumulates entries from failures that have since been fixed, and a stack-doctor pass must decide per-entry whether each one still describes a live condition. On 2026-08-31 the log's entries were confirmed stale, then archived and cleared per the skill's documented procedure.

## Key Points

- **The error log is an escalation channel, not a state record.** Scheduled tasks write to it because no session exists at run time; entries persist until manually cleared regardless of whether the underlying failure was resolved.
- **Clearing requires a staleness determination first.** Each entry must be checked against current ground truth — the relevant job's log, the artifact it was supposed to produce — before the log is emptied, or a live failure is silently discarded.
- **Archive, then clear.** The procedure preserves the entries elsewhere rather than deleting them outright, keeping the failure history available while restoring the log's signal value for the next session.
- **An uncleared log degrades into noise.** Because it is surfaced at every session start, stale entries train the reader to skim past it, which is the same alarm-fatigue dynamic that motivated raising the memsearch session-end alarm threshold from 3 to 6.

## Details

The escalation log exists to solve a specific structural problem: a scheduled job that fails at 06:15 or 09:00 has no session to report to, so it writes to a durable file that the next session start reads. That design makes the log write-only from the job's perspective — nothing in the pipeline knows when a failure has been remediated, so nothing removes the entry. The log therefore represents "failures that were reported at some point," not "failures that are currently true," and any maintenance pass over it is fundamentally a reconciliation task rather than a cleanup task.

The reconciliation is per-entry and requires an independent source. On 2026-08-31 the determination was made by checking the backup log's timeline: the entries corresponded to the 09:00 manifest failure, and the 10:31 re-run had already completed clean, so every entry described a resolved condition. Had any entry lacked such a corroborating success, clearing the log would have erased the only surviving record of an unresolved failure. Archiving before clearing hedges against a wrong staleness call — the entries remain recoverable if a later session discovers the condition was live after all — and it also preserves the failure history for pattern analysis across maintenance passes.

The cost of not doing this is not data loss but signal loss. A log that is displayed at every session start and reliably contains only old, already-fixed entries stops being read, at which point the escalation channel it implements has failed silently while appearing to work. Keeping it empty except when something is genuinely wrong is what makes its non-emptiness informative.

# Vendored Skill Hand-Install Pattern (~/.agents/skills → Claude + Codex)

On 2026-09-04, the `davidondrej/skills` GitHub repository (58 skills) was vetted against the existing environment and five skills were installed by hand after the official `npx skills add` installer was blocked by the auto-mode permission classifier. The session established a working install shape — vendor directory plus two layers of symlink — verified it empirically rather than by assumption, and documented a real cost of the manual route: hand-installed skills are invisible to the upstream lockfile and therefore to `skills update`.

## Key Points

- **53 of 58 skills rejected, with reasons by category:** duplicates of already-installed capability (superpowers, session-handoff, CreateSkill, codex plugin, launchd), dependence on tools absent from this machine (bb, cmux, Herdr, Pi, Cursor, Postgres), a paid DeepAPI key requirement (`risky-changes` and all ten `research-and-web` skills), and hardcoding of the author's own name (`file-tree`, `stop-overthinking`, `short`, `remind`).
- **Five installed, taking the count 151 → 156:** `persistent-localhost` (runs dev servers as launchd jobs, replacing `&`/`nohup`), `anti-sleep` (`caffeinate` for long or overnight runs), and three slash-only skills — `/decisions`, `/before-building`, `/next-decision`.
- **`global-agent-guardrails` was skipped for a concrete conflict,** not redundancy alone: `dcg` already covers the ground, and the skill's denylist blocks `security find-generic-password`, which the Fireflies key read depends on.
- **The working install shape:** copy `SKILL.md` plus `scripts/` and `agents/` into `~/.agents/skills/<name>/`, `chmod +x` the scripts, symlink *relatively* into `~/.claude/skills/<name>`, then symlink `~/.codex/skills/<name>` at `~/.claude/skills/<name>` — every Codex entry points at the Claude path, not at `~/.agents/skills` directly.
- **Hand-installed skills are absent from `~/.agents/.skill-lock.json`,** so `skills update` will not see them. Registering them retroactively is possible by running the official installer behind a `!` prefix to bypass the classifier; it may simply report "already installed."
- **Both installs were tested, not assumed:** `persistent-localhost` served a real HTTP 200 on port 5199 and stopped cleanly; `anti-sleep` reached `ASSERTIONS=active` and stopped leaving no stray plists.

## Details

The vetting ratio — 5 accepted out of 58 — is the substantive finding, and the four rejection categories are reusable as a triage rubric for any third-party skill bundle. Duplication is the largest bucket and the cheapest to check, since an existing capability makes the new skill pure listing overhead against the description budget documented in [[concepts/skill-description-budget-ceiling]]. Missing-dependency and paid-key rejections are hard constraints discoverable by reading the skill body. The author-name-hardcoding category is the least obvious and the most instructive: a skill written for personal use may embed its author's identity in prompts or paths, which makes it silently wrong rather than broken when installed elsewhere. The `global-agent-guardrails` rejection is a fifth, sharper category — active interference, where the skill's denylist would have broken an unrelated working integration (the Fireflies keychain read). That is a case where "we already have coverage" understates the reason to decline.

The symlink topology is worth stating precisely because it is not the obvious arrangement. The canonical files live once in `~/.agents/skills/<name>/`; `~/.claude/skills/<name>` is a *relative* symlink into that directory; and `~/.codex/skills/<name>` symlinks to the Claude path rather than to the vendor path. Routing Codex through Claude rather than pointing both harnesses at the vendor directory means the Claude path is the single indirection point — moving or replacing the underlying skill requires updating one link, not two. The insistence on a relative link for the Claude leg matters given this environment's history with committed symlinks: absolute links that encode a home directory are exactly what broke during the Windows→Mac migration described in [[concepts/committed-symlink-repo-landmine]].

The lockfile gap is the genuine cost of hand-installing and should be recorded wherever the install is documented. `~/.agents/.skill-lock.json` is the manifest `skills update` consults, so a skill installed outside the installer is functionally present but permanently unmanaged — it will never receive an upstream fix. This is the same silent-omission shape as a backup manifest that does not list a folder: every managed item reports success, and the unmanaged item is invisible precisely because nothing knows to look for it. The offered remedy (re-running the official installer behind `!` purely to register the entries) resolves the bookkeeping without repeating the file operations. A final procedural note from the same session: two prior claims recorded in `project_vendored-skill-install.md` were disproven during this work and corrected in Tier A memory, which is the correct disposition for memory that testing contradicts.

# Machine-Restore Closeout and Handoff Note

The 2026-08-11 end-of-day session closed out a multi-day machine-restore checklist: an SSD backup baseline, a Zotero CLI/MCP bundle installation, cleanup of a failed-run artifact, and a written handoff note committed to the global-memory repository. The closeout distinguishes between items genuinely finished, items intentionally left to drain on their own schedule, and items deliberately parked.

## Key Points

- **Handoff artifact:** `~/.claude/global-memory/handoffs/2026-08-06-restore-closeout.md`, committed and pushed — a durable, versioned record of restore state rather than a memory-tier entry.
- **Zotero MCP registered user-scope:** binary at `~/go/bin/zotero-research-library-pp-mcp`, registered as `zotero`; bundle at `~/printing-press/library/zotero-research-library/zotero-research-library.mcpb`.
- **Backup baseline closed:** first full `CRASHBOX` run completed clean (OK, 0 errors, 21:25).
- **Self-draining items are not blockers.** The compiler backlog of 54 daily logs drains on the nightly schedule; PR monitors for #1667 and #1668 were intentionally left stopped because the ball is on the maintainer's side.
- **Parked items carried forward unchanged:** `GMAIL_APP_PASSWORD`, Milvus, and skill-tax — the same three items parked during the 2026-08-06 loose-ends sweep, confirming they remain deliberate deferrals rather than forgotten work.

## Details

The closeout illustrates a three-way classification that keeps an end-of-day review honest. The first class is genuinely complete work with a verifiable artifact: the backup ran clean and produced a receipt, the MCP binary was registered and its bundle staged, and the handoff note was committed and pushed. The second class is work that is neither done nor blocking because a scheduled process will drain it without attention — the 54-log compiler backlog is the canonical example, since the nightly compile job consumes it incrementally, so listing it as an action item would misrepresent it as requiring human effort. The third class is work owned by someone else or explicitly deferred: PRs #1667 and #1668 sit with the maintainer, so the background monitors watching them were stopped rather than left running to generate noise.

The parked trio — `GMAIL_APP_PASSWORD`, Milvus, and skill-tax — is notable for having been carried unchanged since the 2026-08-06 sweep. Restating them at closeout rather than dropping them preserves the distinction between a deliberate deferral and an item that quietly fell off the list; a parked item that stops appearing in closeouts becomes indistinguishable from forgotten work. Routing the whole picture into a committed handoff file under `~/.claude/global-memory/handoffs/` rather than into a memory tier reflects the same routing discipline documented elsewhere: durable state that already has a natural on-disk home should live there, with memory reserved for pointers and conventions. Stopping the PR monitors also aligns with the finding that background monitor events are unreliable — a monitor left running against work that cannot progress produces duplicate or spurious notifications rather than signal.

# Stack Doctor Sweep (2026-08-11): Self-Inflicted Repo Divergence and a Lying Dry Run

A `/claude-stack-doctor` run on 2026-08-11 after a three-day gap took the automation/memory stack from 8 issues to 6 (three of the remaining six being lagging indicators that clear on the next nightly backup). The sweep's most valuable findings were not the fixes themselves but three cases where the *monitoring layer* was the defect: a nightly backup that committed its own generated files and so diverged a repo every night, a `skill-tax` check measuring the wrong quantity, and a `-DryRun` flag that reported git operations it never performed.

## Key Points

- **`repo-diverged:skills` was self-inflicted.** Six tracked files were regenerated every run (`last-weekly-run.log` plus five `__pycache__` entries), so the nightly backup committed churn and diverged the repo nightly. Untracking and gitignoring them was the sweep's highest-leverage fix.
- **`daily-backup.ps1 -DryRun` was lying.** The `Log` calls at lines 28/38 sat *outside* the `if (-not $DryRun)` guards at 24/34, so a dry run printed "committed / pushed" for git operations it never ran — briefly fooling the sweep itself. Fixed to `[dry-run] would commit`.
- **`skill-tax` was a false positive from the monitor's own logic:** it counted all 133 on-disk `SKILL.md` files with no knowledge of `skillOverrides`. Verified empirically first (0 of 72 overridden skills leak into the listing; 61 expected, 60 seen), *then* the script was patched — the two candidate fixes were opposite, so the discriminating check had to precede either.
- **`flush-error` recurrence across 8/08 and 8/11 indicated version skew, not contention:** `claude-agent-sdk` was 26 versions behind (0.2.110 → 0.2.136); upgrading restored flushes, and the memsearch flush patch was confirmed to survive the package operation.
- **Both sides preserved on a two-writer conflict.** Four SecondBrain morning briefings differed from committed origin versions; origin's won by default and are live, with local copies staged at `doctor-backup-20260807-135924/secondbrain-local-briefings/*.local.md` — fully reversible rather than adjudicated on the spot.

## Details

The three monitoring-layer defects share a structure worth naming: each produced a confident, well-formatted signal about a system state it was not actually measuring. The dry-run bug is the purest form — logging placed outside the guard it describes means the flag's entire purpose (previewing without acting) is silently void, and the operator's trust in the preview is inversely related to its accuracy. `skill-tax` is the same failure one level up: the check counted files on disk, a proxy that was correct before `skillOverrides` existed and became wrong afterward, so a previously-completed cleanup appeared not to have landed. The correct response in that case was explicitly *not* to fix either candidate immediately, because the two possible remedies (clean up more skills, or patch the counter) pointed in opposite directions; running the discriminating check first — do overridden skills leak into the listing? — decided which. The `repo-diverged:skills` case is the automation eating its own output: a backup job that commits generated artifacts guarantees divergence on every run, making a real alarm fire nightly for a cause the alarm cannot describe.

The sweep's restraint is as instructive as its fixes. Several issues were deliberately left alone with reasons recorded: 73 unversioned skill files (a design fork — adding `~/.agents/skills` to `backup-manifest.json` was proposed but not applied), unmanaged `DEV` directories (the user's scope call), a 4-log compiler backlog (self-healing at 2/night against ~1/day, and forcing it costs real money), and `snapshot:sessions` (an rsync race against a live Codex file, not rot). Two items were escalated as genuinely not auto-fixable and left open: Outlook auth expired, so morning briefings were shipping with 0 email threads pending an interactive `reauth.sh` run, and Google Drive 154h stale, with files reaching the local `G:` cache but GoogleDriveFS not syncing. The `MEMORY.md` file was at 100% — the next write would have failed — and was consolidated to 93% by shortening wording while keeping all 16 threads, rather than dropping any. Finally, two `flush-error` session IDs were classified benign only after evidence (the IDs exist nowhere; the DEV slug holds 28 transcripts, 3 in the last 24h), on the explicit principle of not classifying by inference; and two self-corrections were made before reporting (an "8 → 2" claim against a raw verdict of 6, and a claim that the /doctor changes were unversioned when the nightly backup had in fact committed them).

# End-of-Day Structured Interview Workflow

A structured end-of-day interview workflow was demonstrated on 2026-05-29, combining a Fireflies meeting sync, a 4-question daily debrief, targeted vault note creation, and global memory system updates (USER.md and MEMORY.md). The session also revealed a critical USER.md character cap constraint and clarified the Tier A vs. Tier B memory split for active vs. durable information.

## Key Points

- **4-question interview format** covers all active projects and workstreams in a single pass, surfacing insights across areas that might otherwise receive no end-of-day attention. The 2026-05-29 run spanned: Dropback vendor call, Jeremy presentation prep, Hoff/Soto AI discovery call, ACWR tennis project, Fall Camp simulator scoping, spirit and cheer summer packet, research database, and upcoming Databricks call.
- **Q4 ("tell a peer one thing") consistently produces the sharpest material:** this prompt forces compression — the user must identify the single transmissible insight from the day. On 2026-05-29 it surfaced: "effort put into answering questions that haven't been asked is in vain" (essay seed), and the connected observation that AI adoption/consensus is the real bottleneck, not direction.
- **Connect interview outputs to existing vault notes rather than creating isolated ones:** updating the existing `self-authored-direction` note with a reframed open question (linking direction to adoption) compounds value more than creating a standalone new note. The connection is the knowledge, not just the content.
- **USER.md cap (1,375 chars):** the global USER.md profile is essentially at capacity (1,370/1,375 as of 2026-05-29). Any future profile addition requires consolidating or pruning existing entries before adding new content — USER.md must be treated as a fixed-size buffer, not an append-only log.
- **MEMORY.md Tier A vs. Tier B:** durable facts about the user go in Tier A; active, fluid threads (e.g., career-pivot consideration) go in Tier B. A Tier B entry signals "this is worth tracking but not yet stable enough to become a fact."
- **Fireflies integration:** new meetings are synced, renamed from generic timestamps to descriptive titles (e.g., `2026-05-28_Eric_and_Jeremy_presentation_prep`), and exported to the vault at `Inbox/meetings/YYYY-MM-DD_<title>.md`.

## Details

The structured end-of-day interview functions as a compression mechanism: a full day of meetings, decisions, and half-formed thoughts is distilled into a small set of high-signal outputs — a vault note, a memory update, an essay seed — without requiring the user to decide in the moment what is worth capturing. By following a fixed question format, the interview ensures consistent coverage across all active workstreams rather than capturing only what was most recent or most emotionally salient. The structure also makes the interview reproducible across sessions and assistants: the same prompt set can be run by any AI instance with access to the user's project context and yield comparable coverage.

The Q4 prompt is architecturally different from the preceding questions because it forces a different cognitive operation. Questions 1–3 surface facts and status updates (what happened, what decisions were made, what is blocked); Q4 forces synthesis and compression — the user must identify the single insight worth transmitting to a peer. This compression step often reveals insights that would not have surfaced through status-update prompts alone. On 2026-05-29, both outputs from Q4 were routed to vault notes rather than MEMORY.md, because they are essay seeds and framing questions rather than durable facts about the user's preferences or context. The distinction matters: MEMORY.md stores facts that help a future AI session orient quickly ("user works at Baylor Athletics"), while vault notes store ideas that the user may want to develop, publish, or return to. AI-adoption/consensus was explicitly deferred to the weekly review rather than drafted immediately — the weekly review is the right context for framing the evidence, finding allies, and deciding whether the idea is worth writing.

# Automation Stack Doctor and Self-Maintaining Scheduled-Task Cycle

The automation stack doctor is a health-check routine that verifies the full local Claude Code automation and memory stack — scheduled tasks, Python venvs, memsearch, Docker/Milvus, the error log, backups, and the Google Drive API heartbeat — and reports a consolidated status. On 2026-07-27, following a Windows reboot, a post-restart stack doctor run returned ALL CLEAR, and the session restructured the stack into a self-maintaining nightly cycle: heavy reindexing was moved into the 6:15 AM backup task while the session-end hook stays a light 45-second incremental pass.

## Key Points

- **Stack doctor scope:** a single run validates all 4 scheduled tasks, Python venvs, memsearch, Docker/Milvus survival across restart, error-log cleanliness, backup freshness, and a Google Drive API heartbeat. The 2026-07-27 post-restart run returned ALL CLEAR (backups fresh at 3h, Milvus survived reboot).
- **Self-deleting post-restart check:** a one-shot scheduled task (`KeystoneOS-PostRestartCheck`, triggered at logon + 5 min) auto-runs stack doctor after a reboot, escalates any failures to `.errors.log`, and deletes itself. This is the workaround for the fact that a session cannot literally wait through a machine restart — failures surface at the next session start via the error log.
- **Nightly reindex folded into the 6:15 AM backup task** (`daily-backup.ps1`): uncapped, uses the full `memsearch.exe` path (per the Task Scheduler PATH lesson), escalates per-path failures, and resets the hook timeout-streak counter on success. Rationale: a first-time SecondBrain book-library index is an hours-scale job that a 45-second session-end hook can never absorb.
- **Backup task execution limit raised 30 min → 2 h** so a heavy reindex night is not killed mid-pass. The session-end hook stays light (45 s incremental) and its alarm threshold was raised 3 → 6 so it only alarms if the nightly safety net itself falls behind — a real signal, not noise.
- **Cloud-check timezone bug fixed:** a "-4h old" false backup-freshness reading came from timestamps not normalized to UTC after `ConvertFrom-Json`; the check now normalizes to UTC regardless of the return type.

## Details

The session's central move is an architectural relocation of expensive work off the interactive/hook path and onto a scheduled job. The recurring memsearch indexing alarm had been misdiagnosed the prior day as an "occasional" hiccup; on 2026-07-27 it was recognized as structural — a first-time embedding job measured in hours (one indexer had burned 81 CPU-minutes and was still running). Because a 45-second session-end hook can never complete an hours-scale index, the correct home for that work is the nightly 6:15 AM `daily-backup.ps1` task, which runs uncapped and escalates per-path failures. The session-end hook is left as a light incremental pass, and its alarm threshold is raised from 3 to 6 consecutive misses so it only fires when the nightly safety net itself falls behind. With the library index converging over a night or two while search stays live, the alarm becomes a meaningful signal rather than chronic noise.

Two supporting reliability fixes accompanied the restructure. The backup task's execution time limit was raised from 30 minutes to 2 hours so a heavy reindex night is not terminated mid-pass — a scheduled job that runs an unbounded index needs an execution ceiling wide enough to absorb the worst case. The cloud-check UTC normalization fix addressed a false "-4h old" reading: after `ConvertFrom-Json`, timestamps were being compared without normalizing to UTC, so a local-vs-UTC offset was misread as staleness; normalizing regardless of the parsed return type eliminated the false alarm. The `KeystoneOS-PostRestartCheck` self-deleting task closes the post-reboot verification gap — because no session can survive a restart, a one-shot logon-triggered task that runs stack doctor and escalates to `.errors.log` is the mechanism by which post-restart health reaches the user at the next session start. All changes were committed and pushed to the dotclaude and skills repos with no pending user action; the first fully self-maintaining cycle (backup → snapshot → reindex → alarm reset) was scheduled to run the following morning at 6:15 AM.

## Related Concepts

- [[concepts/memsearch-tool-maintenance]] — The memsearch tool whose hours-scale first-index drove this restructure; the nightly reindex-in-backup-task architecture and the raised 3→6 alarm threshold are documented there as well.
- [[concepts/windows-task-scheduler-path-config]] — The full-`memsearch.exe`-path requirement applied to the nightly reindex task is a direct application of this Task Scheduler minimal-PATH lesson.
- [[concepts/in-session-background-process-limits]] — The architectural rationale for moving hours-scale reindexing out of the session entirely: long-running background commands do not survive a session, so scheduled jobs are their correct home.

# Claude Code Three-Tier Memory Architecture

The Claude Code memory system is composed of three independent layers, each operating at a different granularity and owned by a different mechanism. This architecture was articulated on 2026-05-19 during a session that traced exactly when and how each capture mechanism fires. On 2026-06-05, a practical capacity-management routing pattern emerged for when Tier B global memory approaches its character cap. On 2026-06-18, a worked example clarified how to route a specific piece of context across the tiers — and which content should not enter the memory system at all.

## Key Points

- **Tier A — Native Claude Code auto-memory:** Built into Claude Code itself; managed per-project; no user configuration required. Operates automatically within a project context; its exact retention and synthesis mechanics are not user-visible.
- **Tier B — Custom global scratchpad via Stop hook:** A user-configured hook on the `Stop` event, which fires after every conversation turn. This provides incremental, per-turn transcript capture to a global scratchpad file (MEMORY.md) — a granularity that neither Tier A nor Tier C provides.
- **Tier C — claude-memory-compiler:** The [[concepts/claude-memory-compiler-setup]] system: `SessionEnd` and `PreCompact` hooks fire shell commands at session teardown or auto-compaction, spawning a detached `flush.py` process that appends structured notes to the daily log; at end-of-day these are compiled into knowledge articles.
- **The agent never sees a "session ending" event.** Session end and compaction are harness-level events; it is the Claude Code harness that runs the hook shell commands, not the agent itself.
- **PreCompact as a safety net:** In a long session with multiple auto-compactions, PreCompact fires before each one, preventing total context loss if the session later crashes before `SessionEnd`.
- **When Tier B is near cap, route to Tier A project files:** The global MEMORY.md (Tier B) has a character-cap constraint. When it approaches capacity, new durable facts should be saved to Tier A project-specific memory files (e.g., `project_<name>.md`, `user_career_timeline.md`), which are cross-project searchable via memsearch.
- **Content-to-tier routing matrix (2026-06-18):** file locations and versioning decisions belong in Tier B as an active-thread entry ("continue this next session"); durable personal conventions (e.g. "always save v1 before editing") belong in Tier A as a feedback rule; and the actual artifact content (slides, scripts) should NOT be duplicated in memory at all because it already lives on disk. Tier C's daily-log capture provides a compressed "what did I do that day" summary but is not a substitute for a durable artifact reference.

## Details

The three tiers are designed to capture context at different time horizons and granularities, and they operate independently rather than hierarchically. Tier A is fully opaque to the user. Tier B's Stop-hook scratchpad is the most granular: because the Stop event fires after every conversation turn, Tier B can capture mid-session context incrementally in near-real-time. Tier C produces the richest synthesized output — compiled knowledge articles from daily logs — but fires only at session boundaries.

The independence of the three tiers is their key reliability property. A failure in one does not cascade to the others: if a session crashes before `SessionEnd` fires, the Stop-hook's Tier B scratchpad may still contain the session's important turns. The "agent never sees session ending" detail is architecturally important: code written inside the agent context cannot detect or react to its own session ending. Teardown logic must be placed in hook shell commands that the harness executes.

The Tier B near-cap routing pattern (2026-06-05) addresses a practical capacity constraint. The correct response when Tier B is near capacity is not to compress existing entries — which risks discarding information encoded in current phrasing — but to route new durable facts into named Tier A project memory files, which are surfaced by memsearch across all project contexts.

The 2026-06-18 worked example makes the routing decision concrete and, importantly, identifies content that should stay out of memory entirely. Asked how best to preserve a working session's context (an RTP presentation's file locations, a v1/v2 versioning decision, and the slides/script themselves), the assistant produced a routing matrix rather than dumping everything into one tier: the file paths and versioning state map to Tier B because they describe an active thread to resume next session; a general preference like "always save v1 before editing" maps to Tier A as a durable feedback rule; and the actual slide and script content maps to neither — it already exists as files on disk, so copying it into memory would only create a stale duplicate. The distinction matters because the memory system's value is in cheap-to-retrieve pointers and rules, not in re-storing artifacts that a file path already addresses. The same example noted that Tier C's automatic daily-log capture is a lossy summary ("good for what did I do that day, not great for pick up exactly where I left off"), reinforcing that a deliberate Tier B pointer is the right tool when the goal is precise session continuity.

# Backup Manifest Drift and Stale launchd Exit Status

On 2026-08-31 a `/claude-stack-doctor` health check investigated a failed 09:00 `com.keystone.dailybackup` run and traced it to three project folders missing from the hand-maintained backup manifest. The manifest was corrected at 10:31, the backup re-ran immediately and completed with 0 errors, but `launchctl list` continued to report a non-zero exit code because that column reflects only the last *scheduled* run. The session established both a new failure mode (manifest omission, distinct from the documented `backup-*` classes) and a diagnostic rule for reading launchd status against the backup log timeline.

## Key Points

- **Manifest omission is its own failure class.** Three project folders were absent from the backup manifest; the job surfaced this as `backup-error` with per-folder entries in `daily-backup.log`, not as any of the previously documented `backup-*` failure classes.
- **`launchctl list` column 2 reports the last *scheduled* run only.** Manual or out-of-band re-runs do not update it, so a green `daily-backup.log` and a red launchd status can coexist without contradiction.
- **Confirm against the log timeline before treating an exit code as live.** The correct ground truth for "is the backup healthy right now?" is the most recent run's log entry, not the launchd status field.
- **A stale exit code is left to self-clear.** The recommendation was to do nothing rather than force-run the job: the next 09:00 scheduled run overwrites the status, and a manual re-run would change only the cosmetic field, not any real state.
- **Hand-maintained manifests drift.** The recorded follow-up question is whether the manifest should be auto-derived from `~/.claude/projects` rather than curated by hand, removing the omission failure mode at its source.

## Details

The manifest omission is a coverage failure rather than an execution failure, which is why it does not fit the existing `backup-*` taxonomy. Every path the job was told to back up succeeded; the defect is that three paths were never in the instruction set. This class is silent by construction — a backup whose scope is wrong still reports per-folder success for the folders it knows about, and only the aggregate `backup-error` plus the per-folder entries in `daily-backup.log` expose the gap. The proposed remedy of deriving the manifest from `~/.claude/projects` rather than maintaining it by hand converts an omission that requires human vigilance into one that requires a directory scan, which is the same move as replacing an inferred boundary with a declared one elsewhere in this stack.

The launchd status lag is a distinct lesson about which signal counts as ground truth. `launchctl list` exposes the exit status of the daemon's own last invocation of the job, so any run initiated outside the schedule — a manual invocation, an interactive re-run during a diagnostic session — leaves that field untouched. The consequence is a persistent false-red: the system is healthy, the log proves it, and the status field will disagree until the next scheduled tick. The correct response is to read the status field as a timestamped historical claim and reconcile it against the backup log's timeline, exactly as background-task exit codes must be reconciled against on-disk artifacts before being believed. Force-running the job to clear the field would be treating the display as the state.

Both findings reinforce that this backup subsystem accumulates its failures at the reporting layer rather than the data layer. The snapshots themselves were fine in the 2026-08-06 receipt-race incident, fine here after the manifest fix, and the recurring diagnostic work is about which of several disagreeing signals — receipt read-back, launchd exit code, per-folder log entries — actually describes the backup's state.

## Related Concepts

- [[concepts/launchd-backup-receipt-race-repo-reconciliation]] — The same backup job under `launchd`; there the misleading signal was a receipt read-back racing Drive's write-lag, here it is a status field scoped to scheduled runs only.
- [[concepts/automation-stack-doctor]] — The health-check routine that surfaced both issues; backup freshness is one of its standing checks.
- [[concepts/crashbox-ssd-backup-baseline]] — The local SSD leg written by this same manifest; documents that the manifest tolerates paths with spaces and that rsync makes restarts incremental.

- [[connections/verify-before-trusting-tool-output]] — The broader discipline of checking ground truth rather than the layer reporting on it.

# Baylor Load Simulator: Vercel Deployment and Navigation

The Baylor Load Simulator app was deployed to Vercel production on 2026-04-14, fixing a server/client date-serialization bug along the way and adding persistent navigation between its `/reference` (Reference Card) and `/admin` (GPS Sync) pages. Active feature development continued into May 2026, including a Projected-vs-Actual comparison view and ongoing work to reconcile the app's data model with Catapult's real-world sync behavior.

## Key Points

- Neon (serverless Postgres) returns `practice_date` and `synced_at` columns as native JS `Date` objects rather than strings; these had to be serialized to ISO strings in the API routes before being passed to React client components.
- The Vercel project was not yet linked, so the MCP deploy tool could not deploy directly - `npx vercel link` had to be run interactively in a separate terminal first, as a one-time prerequisite.
- The `CATAPULT_TOKEN` value could not be pasted directly into chat (likely due to special characters); the workaround was to add it to `.env.local`, then have the assistant read the file and push the value to Vercel via the CLI.
- A persistent dark navigation bar was added to the authenticated layout, linking to the previously-unlinked `/reference` and `/admin` pages; it is hidden on `/login` and visible on all authenticated pages. A third top-level tab, `/comparison`, was planned on 2026-05-12 to surface the new Projected-vs-Actual comparison view (see [[concepts/baylor-load-simulator-comparison-view]]).
- `.vercel/` remains gitignored per standard practice (the project link itself is not committed), and `CLAUDE.md` was updated with the simulator's architecture, known gotchas, and deploy commands for future sessions.

## Details

The Neon date-serialization issue is a reusable lesson beyond this one app: any Next.js project querying Neon (or other Postgres providers using the `pg`/`@neondatabase/serverless` drivers) should expect timestamp/date columns to come back as JS `Date` objects, which are not directly serializable across the server-to-client component boundary. The fix - explicitly converting these fields to ISO strings inside API routes before they reach client components - resolved the deployment-blocking error.

Two pages, the Reference Card (`/reference`) and GPS Sync (`/admin`), existed in the codebase but had no way to reach them from the UI; adding the nav bar made them discoverable. The GPS Sync panel is functionally complete but not yet useful in practice - it will only become "live" once Catapult has actual GPS data for the practice dates being tested, which ties this deployment to the broader, ongoing challenge of getting reliable Catapult data into Baylor Athletics' various tools. Outstanding work includes connecting GitHub auto-deploy (Vercel dashboard, Settings > Git, with root directory set to `simulator`) so future pushes to `main` deploy automatically without a manual CLI step.

A month later, on 2026-05-12, development resumed with a `ComparisonChart` feature overlaying projected vs. actual practice load on `/practices/[id]/compare`, plus a confirmed plan to promote it to a top-level `/comparison` nav tab (see [[concepts/baylor-load-simulator-comparison-view]]). Building that chart surfaced a Catapult sync-aggregation issue - the same period type ("1 ON 1") appearing twice, non-adjacently, in a single practice's data - which the team chose to leave aggregated for now rather than redesign the sync model mid-season (see [[concepts/catapult-period-aggregation-sync-policy]]). This is the same recurring theme as the GPS Sync panel's dependency on Catapult data: the app's data model and Catapult's actual data don't always line up cleanly, and reconciling them is an ongoing, incremental process rather than a one-time fix.

## Related Concepts

# Committed Symlinks in the Wrong Repo with core.symlinks=false

On 2026-08-08, a `git reset --hard origin/main` on `~/.agents/skills` corrupted all 21 mattpocock skills. The root cause is a structural landmine: 21 symlinks that logically belong to `~/.claude/skills` are committed into the *wrong* repository (`~/.agents/skills`) as git mode `120000` entries with self-referential targets (`../../.agents/skills/<name>`), while that checkout has inherited `core.symlinks=false` from its Windows origin. Under that configuration, any `checkout`, `reset`, or `stash` writes each symlink out as a ~29-byte plain text file containing the target path, silently breaking all 21 skills.

## Key Points

- **The mechanism:** git stores a symlink as a blob whose contents are the target path, with file mode `120000`. When `core.symlinks=false`, git materializes that blob as a regular file containing the path text (~29 bytes) instead of creating an actual symlink. Every skill then resolves to a text file rather than a directory.
- **`core.symlinks=false` is inherited from Windows:** git sets this automatically on Windows checkouts where symlink creation requires elevated privileges. The setting persists in `.git/config` after a migration to macOS, where symlinks would otherwise work fine — so the constraint outlives the platform that justified it.
- **Wrong-repo commit compounds it:** the 21 symlinks belong to `~/.claude/skills` but are tracked in `~/.agents/skills`, and their targets are self-referential (`../../.agents/skills/<name>`). Because `origin/main` tracks these paths as symlinks, they are not "local-only files" that a reset would leave alone.
- **It re-breaks on every history-touching operation:** this is not a one-time corruption. `checkout`, `reset`, and `stash` all re-materialize the working tree from the index, so each one re-writes the 21 symlinks as text — a recurring landmine, not a fixed bug.
- **Proposed fix (two parts):** deliberately commit the *deletion* of the 21 bogus self-referential symlinks, **and** set `core.symlinks=true` on the `~/.agents/skills` checkout so git stops materializing symlinks as text. Either half alone leaves the trap partially armed.
- **Recovery on 2026-08-08:** restored from `agents-skills-before-reset.tar.gz`; HEAD returned to `459c9ba` (= `origin/main`), all 21 symlinks resolving and 133 `SKILL.md` files reachable. Backups preserved in `~/.claude/doctor-backup-20260807-135924/` (`agents-skills-before-codex-fix.tar.gz` pre-sed, `agents-skills-before-reset.tar.gz` post-restore).

## Details

The failure is a three-factor interaction, and no single factor is individually alarming. Factor one: symlinks are tracked in git at all, which is normal and supported. Factor two: `core.symlinks=false`, which is a reasonable and automatic default on Windows. Factor three: the symlinks are committed in a repository that is not their logical home, with targets that point back into that same repository's own path. Individually each is defensible; together they mean that the repository's normal operations are destructive to the thing the repository is supposed to be serving. The corruption is silent — no error, no warning, just 21 directories replaced by 29-byte text files — and only surfaces when a skill fails to load.

An important secondary finding is that the agent's prediction of `reset --hard` behavior was wrong. The prediction was that 76 local-only files would survive the reset; in fact 73 did not, precisely because `origin/main` tracks those paths as symlinks rather than treating them as untracked. Files that appear local-only from a working-tree perspective may be tracked upstream under a different file type, and a `--hard` reset will overwrite them. This mispredicted-blast-radius outcome validated the practice of pausing for explicit user review before destructive git operations on this repository — a discipline that paid for itself here, since the pre-reset tarball is what made recovery possible.

The remediation must address both the wrong-repo tracking and the configuration. Committing the deletion of the 21 self-referential symlinks removes them from the index, so future checkouts have nothing bogus to materialize. Setting `core.symlinks=true` ensures that any *legitimate* symlink in the tree is created as a real symlink on macOS rather than as text. The fix carries a scheduling hazard: the nightly `daily-backup` job auto-commits `~/.agents/skills`, so if it runs before a decision is made it will commit and push the deletion unattended. The deletion happens to be the correct action, but shipping it unreviewed through an automated job is a different risk profile than shipping it deliberately — which is why the item was flagged as time-sensitive against the nightly run.
