# A Router Pointing at a Wrong Answer: Stale DEV Memory After the Mac Migration

The sharpest finding of the 2026-09-02 memlint run was structural rather than factual. `project_dev-layout-and-discovery.md` still claimed the `DEV` directory lived at `~/Desktop/DEV` — a Windows-era layout — while `DEV/CLAUDE.md` explicitly routed all layout questions *to that file*. The wrong fact was therefore not merely present in memory; it was the designated authority on its own topic. Roughly eight DEV memory files carried similar Windows-era claims, and all of them loaded into every session.

## Key Points

- **Delegation multiplies the cost of a stale fact.** A wrong claim sitting in an unreferenced file is one bad data point; a wrong claim in a file that another document names as the canonical source is the answer to every question on that topic.
- **The stale claim survived the platform that produced it.** `~/Desktop/DEV` was correct on Windows and became wrong on macOS, with nothing in the migration path that would notice or flag the discrepancy.
- **Scale matters: ~8 DEV memory files carried Windows-era claims, and they loaded every session.** Unlike a stale file on disk that is read only when opened, memory-tier staleness is paid on every conversation.
- **Establishing a canonical pointer creates an obligation to verify the target.** `DEV/CLAUDE.md`'s routing line was itself correct and useful; the defect was that nothing re-checked the pointed-at content after the host changed.
- **This is what made stale memories the higher-priority cleanup** over the 23 broken `[[links]]`: a broken link fails loudly and resolves to nothing, while a stale router answers confidently and wrongly.

## Details

The failure has the same root as the other Windows-artifact survivals catalogued in [[connections/windows-defaults-outlive-the-windows-machine]]: a fact captured at one moment on one host, frozen into a durable artifact, and never re-verified when the host changed underneath it. What distinguishes this instance is the routing layer. Canonical-source pointers are a good pattern — they prevent the same fact from being restated in five places and drifting apart — but they concentrate risk, because the correctness of every consumer now depends on the correctness of one target. The relocation discipline in [[concepts/canonical-section-relocation-inbound-pointers]] deals with the same coupling from the other direction, where moving a canonical section leaves inbound pointers dangling; here the pointer resolves fine and delivers a wrong answer, which is strictly harder to detect.

Memory-tier staleness is also more expensive than ordinary file staleness because of when it is read. A stale README costs something only when someone opens it. A stale memory file that is injected at session start is consulted implicitly in every conversation, shaping paths, assumptions, and tool invocations without ever being displayed for review. Eight such files in the DEV slug means eight Windows-era premises silently in play at the start of every DEV session. That asymmetry is the concrete argument behind the session's option-A-over-option-B choice: broken `[[links]]` degrade retrieval, whereas stale facts degrade reasoning, and the latter fails silently.

The remedy implied by the finding is not a one-time correction but a verification obligation attached to the pointer itself. Wherever one document declares another the authority on a topic, the pair should be re-checked together whenever the underlying environment changes — a migration, a directory reorganization, a tool replacement. Absent that, the routing relationship converts a single stale file into a systematically wrong answer, and the confidence with which it is delivered is proportional to how well the routing was designed.

- [[concepts/canonical-section-relocation-inbound-pointers]] — The complementary hazard for canonical pointers: relocation leaves inbound references dangling rather than wrong.

# A Free Diagnostic Run Overwriting a Paid One

During the 2026-09-02 memlint work, running the free structural-only check overwrote the day's paid LLM contradiction report, because both modes wrote to the same `memlint-YYYY-MM-DD.md` filename. The session described this as a self-inflicted footgun and fixed it by giving the cheap mode its own filename, `memlint-YYYY-MM-DD-structural.md`, so a zero-cost run can never clobber a result that cost money to produce.

## Key Points

- **Two modes of the same tool wrote to one date-keyed path.** The structural check (free) and the full check (LLM-backed, ~$0.15–0.25) shared `memlint-YYYY-MM-DD.md`, so whichever ran last won.
- **The overwrite is asymmetric in cost.** Losing the free report costs seconds of recompute; losing the paid one costs money and, worse, the findings themselves if nobody notices the swap.
- **Silence is what makes it dangerous.** The structural run completes successfully and produces a valid report; nothing indicates that a richer prior result was destroyed.
- **The fix is a distinct output path per mode, not a prompt or a guard.** `--structural-only` now writes `memlint-YYYY-MM-DD-structural.md`, which removes the collision structurally rather than relying on the operator remembering which mode ran first.
- **The generalization: any tool with a cheap mode and an expensive mode must not share an output artifact** — the cheap mode will be run more often, and by default it will win.

## Details

The mechanism is ordinary filename collision, but the reason it is worth recording is the cost asymmetry between the two producers. A tool that offers a fast/free tier and a slow/paid tier invites frequent use of the former; that is the entire point of having the tier. If both tiers write the same artifact, the frequently-run cheap mode will overwrite the rarely-run expensive one as a matter of statistics, and it will do so on the very days when someone is actively working the tool — precisely when the paid findings are most likely to still be needed. The failure is quiet in both directions: the run that destroys the report succeeds, and the report that was destroyed leaves no marker.

The chosen remedy is worth contrasting with the alternatives. A confirmation prompt would place the burden on an operator who has no reason to suspect a conflict; a timestamped-filename scheme would prevent the overwrite but scatter reports and break the "today's report" convention that makes the date key useful. Encoding the *mode* into the filename keeps the date-key convention, keeps exactly one artifact per mode per day, and makes the two results readable side by side — which is itself informative, since the structural findings are a subset that the LLM run does not repeat. This is the same corrective shape as writing generated artifacts to durable rather than disposable paths in [[concepts/scratch-folder-artifact-durability]]: the fix removes the decision point rather than adding a rule to remember.

The finding also belongs to this environment's running theme of reporting-layer defects. The backup subsystem's failures in [[concepts/backup-manifest-drift-and-launchd-status-lag]] and the dry-run and `skill-tax` bugs in [[concepts/stack-doctor-sweep-2026-08-11]] were all cases where the monitored systems were fine and the machinery that reported on them was not. An overwritten report is the same category: the check ran correctly, found real things, and then the record of what it found was destroyed by a sibling process that had no idea it was doing so.

- [[concepts/memlint-memory-tier-cleanup]] — The session where the collision was hit and fixed; documents both memlint modes and their costs.
- [[concepts/scratch-folder-artifact-durability]] — The same class of artifact-loss defect, and the same remedy of changing the default write location rather than adding vigilance.

- [[concepts/backup-manifest-drift-and-launchd-status-lag]] — Another reporting-layer defect in the same automation stack.

# Handoff With Uncommitted Tooling Changes and Cross-Session Uncertainty

The 2026-09-02 memory-hygiene session closed by producing a handoff document via `/mattpocock-skills:handoff`, written to `/var/folders/gw/8qg6y2bj7rvdqzttmxfl9lx00000gn/T/handoff-memlint-2026-09-02.md`. The handoff verified every referenced path and included no secrets, but it also carried forward two unresolved states worth naming: a set of uncommitted changes in the memory-compiler repo deliberately left for the user's decision, and an open question about whether a different session had already fixed a problem this session was about to work on.

## Key Points

- **New tooling was left uncommitted on purpose.** `memlint.py` (new) plus modifications to `config.py`, `weekly-adjudicate.ps1`, `README.md`, and `AGENTS.md` were staged in the working tree but not committed — an explicit user's-call deferral rather than an oversight.
- **The handoff verified paths and excluded secrets** as part of its own production, which is what makes a handoff actionable rather than merely descriptive.
- **The handoff was again written to a temp path** under `/var/folders/.../T/` — the same disposable location repeatedly flagged as a trap, reproduced here for at least the third recorded time.
- **Cross-session uncertainty was recorded as an item, not resolved by assumption:** `project_memsearch-hook-timeout-cap.md` appeared after the prior session, implying another session may already have handled the memsearch ETIMEDOUT failures. The action item is to *check* rather than to fix.
- **An ordering dependency was captured explicitly:** the DEV `name:` frontmatter spelling (whether the `project-` prefix belongs) must be settled before the 23 broken `[[links]]` are repaired, since the link targets depend on the naming decision.

## Details

The uncommitted-tooling deferral is the interesting half. `memlint.py` had just been written, run, and used to drive real edits to memory files, so it was demonstrably functional — yet the session declined to commit it, along with the supporting changes to `config.py`, the weekly adjudication script, and the two documentation files. Deferring the commit to a human decision is defensible when the changes touch a scheduled job's behavior, as `weekly-adjudicate.ps1` does, since committing would put a newly written checker into an automated cadence without review. The cost is the deferral window described in [[concepts/git-sync-status-versus-uncommitted-work]]: until the change set is committed, a repo-sync indicator reporting `ahead=0` says nothing about whether the day's work is preserved, and the only protection is whatever backup leg captures uncommitted files.

The memsearch item demonstrates a distinct discipline for multi-session environments. The evidence — a memory file that appeared after the previous session ended — is suggestive but not conclusive, and the two possible responses (fix it again, or assume it is handled) are both wrong in one direction. Recording it as "check whether this is already handled" preserves the observation without committing to either duplicate work or a silent gap, which is the same reconciliation instinct applied to background-task exit codes in [[connections/background-task-exit-code-false-failure]]. In an environment where multiple sessions write to shared memory and tooling, the appearance of an unfamiliar artifact is a signal that another writer exists, and the correct next move is to look rather than infer.

The ordering dependency between the frontmatter naming decision and the broken-link repair is a small but genuinely useful piece of sequencing knowledge. Fixing 23 links against a naming convention that is subsequently changed means fixing them twice; the naming question is cheap and the link repair is not, so the cheap decision goes first. Finally, the handoff's own placement in `/var/folders/.../T/` is a repeat of the trap documented in [[concepts/handoff-document-placement-discipline]] and [[concepts/scratch-folder-artifact-durability]] — a session that carefully verified the paths *inside* its handoff wrote the handoff itself to a location that does not survive a reboot, which is the strongest available argument that the fix must be a durable default rather than attention.

# Compiler Backlog as a Hook-Reported Latency Signal

The session-start hook reports how many daily logs remain uncompiled, surfacing the Tier C compiler's queue depth as a standing notice. On 2026-09-01 it read 7 logs pending against 2 compiled. The signal is one of latency rather than loss — the source daily logs are on disk and immutable, so a backlog delays knowledge availability without endangering the underlying material. On 2026-09-02 the backlog acquired a second consequence: it was identified as the cause of the compiler repo's one failing test, converting a passive queue-depth notice into an active blocker on the test suite.

## Key Points

- **The hook reports queue depth, not failure.** "7 pending, 2 compiled" describes how far behind the compile stage is; the daily logs themselves are already captured and durable.
- **Backlogs in this system are usually self-draining.** The 54-log backlog after the machine restore drained on the nightly schedule without intervention, which is why a pending count is not automatically an action item.
- **A backlog can nonetheless break something downstream.** On 2026-09-02 the uncompiled logs were identified as the cause of the compiler repo's single failing test, which makes draining it a prerequisite for a clean suite rather than a convenience.
- **The manual drain is a one-liner:** `uv run --directory ~/.claude/claude-memory-compiler python scripts/compile.py`.
- **Forcing a drain has a real cost** — each daily log compiles for roughly $0.45–0.65 — so the default of letting the nightly job absorb it is economically as well as operationally correct, absent a downstream blocker.

## Details

The distinction between latency and loss is what makes the hook notice readable. Tier C's value chain runs source log → compiled knowledge article, and only the second half is behind. Because `daily/` is append-only and the compiler tracks SHA-256 hashes in `state.json`, a log that has not yet been compiled will be compiled eventually and will produce the same output whenever it runs. This is structurally unlike a dropped monitor event or an unwritten memory entry, where the material itself is gone. The correct default reading of a nonzero pending count is therefore "knowledge is not yet queryable," not "knowledge was lost" — the same reading applied to the 54-log restore backlog in [[concepts/machine-restore-closeout-handoff]], which was explicitly classified as self-draining rather than as an action item.

The 2026-09-02 addition changes the calculus in a specific and limited way. A failing test in the compiler repo attributable to the backlog means the pending logs are now blocking a verification signal, not just delaying article availability. That is enough to justify a manual run, because a persistently red suite trains the reader to ignore it — the same alarm-fatigue dynamic that motivated raising the memsearch alarm threshold and clearing the stale `.errors.log`. The distinction to hold onto is that the backlog did not become more urgent in itself; it became coupled to something that is urgent, and that coupling is what promotes it from a notice to a task.

Against that sits the cost. Compiling a daily log runs $0.45–0.65 and rises as the knowledge base grows, so seven pending logs is a few dollars of work that the nightly job would otherwise perform for free from the user's perspective — it happens on a schedule either way. The reasonable policy is to let the schedule handle it by default and to force a drain only when something downstream depends on the queue being empty, which is exactly the situation the failing test created.

# Connection: Always-Loaded Context Is the Expensive Place to Be Wrong

## The Connection

Three findings from the same week converge on one property of the memory tier: a fact injected at session start is paid for on every conversation, and its errors compound the same way. `project_dev-layout-and-discovery.md` claimed DEV lived at `~/Desktop/DEV` while `DEV/CLAUDE.md` named it the authority on layout. `~/DEV/CLAUDE.md` carried exact inventory counts that had silently gone stale. And the standing token-cost work — trimming the Tier A index from 15 files to 10, distilling the on-ramp — treats the always-loaded set as the scarce resource it is. Wrongness, staleness, and volume are three costs levied on the same surface.

## Key Insight

Ordinary documents are read on demand; memory files are read unconditionally. That changes the arithmetic of every defect in them. A stale README misleads whoever opens it, once. A stale memory file shapes assumptions in every session silently, without ever being displayed for scrutiny — and if another document routes questions to it, it becomes the confident answer rather than one input among many.

The corrective moves therefore differ from ordinary documentation hygiene in a consistent direction: **reduce the surface, and record what remains at a stability level that outlives change.** The Tier A trim removed four files from auto-injection while leaving them memsearch-retrievable — less resident, no less available. The DEV counts were replaced with rounded figures and a ratio ("about two thirds of DEV") because a ratio decays more slowly than an absolute. And memlint's whole premise is that this surface needs a periodic audit that `lint.py`, which stops at `knowledge/`, never provided.

The routing case is the sharpest, because it inverts the usual assumption that consolidation reduces risk. Naming one canonical source is good practice against drift, but it concentrates the consequence of that source being wrong: every consumer inherits the error at full confidence. Consolidation converts many possibly-inconsistent answers into one authoritative answer, which is an improvement only insofar as the authority is verified. Where a canonical pointer exists, the pointer and its target must be re-checked together whenever the environment they describe changes.

## Evidence

- **2026-09-02:** `project_dev-layout-and-discovery.md` still claimed `~/Desktop/DEV` — a Windows-era path — while `DEV/CLAUDE.md` routed layout questions to it. Roughly 8 DEV memory files carried Windows-era claims that "loaded every session." Stale memories were explicitly prioritized over 23 broken `[[links]]` on the reasoning that stale files "were actively feeding Claude wrong facts."
- **2026-09-07:** Stale inventory counts in `~/DEV/CLAUDE.md` were corrected and then deliberately rounded with `~`, and a raw file pair was rewritten as "about two thirds of DEV" because the ratio outlives the absolutes.
- **2026-06-25:** The Tier A auto-injection index was trimmed 15 → 10 files (~8,800 → ~6,700 tokens per session) with the removed files left on disk and memsearch-searchable — cutting resident cost without cutting retrievability.
- **2026-08-15:** A session-context footprint audit measured ~21.5k tokens always loaded against ~3,000 claimed in `CLAUDE.md`, establishing that the resident set is both larger and less well understood than its own documentation asserts.
